555: ### Discussion
556: 
557: There was a significant escalation in measles transmission in 2024 compared to previous years, highlighted by the 
558: epidemiological data presented above. A total of 35 212 measles cases were reported, resulting in an overall 
559: notification rate of 77.4 cases per 1 000 000 population — a significant increase compared to the 2023 rate of 5.3 
560: per 1 000 000 population. Romania continued to report the highest notification rate, with 1 610.7 cases per 
561: 1 000 000 population, substantially higher than its 2023 rate (92.2 cases per 1 000 000).
562: 
563: The first half of 2024 showed a particularly sharp increase in measles activity, reaching levels higher than any level 
564: recorded over the past two decades, before it declined again toward the end of the year. In response to this rapid 
565: rise in cases, ECDC issued a dedicated Threat Assessment Brief emphasising the ongoing public health risk, 
566: highlighting concerns around sub-optimal vaccination coverage, the high potential for cross-border transmission, 
567: and the anticipated seasonal peak which further compounded the risk [2].
568: 
569: Similar to previous years, measles continued to affect individuals across all age groups in 2024. Infants under one 
570: year of age were the most severely impacted, showing the highest incidence at 1 175.4 cases per 1 000 000 
571: population. This population group remains particularly vulnerable since infants under one year are typically too 
572: young for direct vaccination and thus rely heavily on population immunity for protection. In 2024, 87% of all cases 
573: with known vaccination status were unvaccinated. Among children aged one to four years, who would typically 
574: receive their first dose of measles vaccine in national vaccination schedules, the rate remained high at 688.7 per 
575: 1 000 000 population, with 90% of these children unvaccinated, underlying the fact that ongoing gaps are present 
576: in this critical age group.
577: 
578: The age distribution of measles cases in 2024 reveals a notable difference between the EU/EEA countries. In 
579: Romania, over one-third of all cases were in children aged 1–4 years, while in several other countries (e.g. Italy, 
580: Spain, France, Poland), the majority of cases occurred in adults aged 30 years and older. This difference may
581: indicate variation in vaccination coverage in the age groups over a longer historical period and the gaps in catch-up 
582: vaccination strategies. Romania’s sharp drop in MCV1 and MCV2 coverage over recent years, especially among 
583: young children, likely facilitated early-age transmission [11]. Conversely, in countries with higher current childhood 
584: coverage but missed vaccinations in the past, older cohorts are now more exposed and at risk of infection [12].
585: 
586: Hospitalisation rates for measles cases remained consistently high in 2024, with 79% of reported cases required
587: hospitalisation. This aligns closely with the 2023 hospitalisation rate of 80% but significantly exceeds earlier figures 
588: from preceding years (33% in 2022 and 55% in 2019). Additionally, most hospitalised individuals—approximately 
589: 85% — were unvaccinated. In 2024, complications from measles were frequently reported, predominantly 
590: affecting unvaccinated individuals. Among hospitalised patients, complications such as pneumonia, otitis media, 
591: and encephalitis continued to be prevalent. Importantly, 2024 recorded 23 measles-related deaths (of which 22 
592: were reported from Romania), a marked increase compared to the three fatalities reported in 2023. Notably, 14 
593: deaths were reported in children below the age of five years.
594: 
595: While the majority of measles cases reported in 2024 originated from local transmission within EU/EEA countries, 
596: among the cases with known importation status, 18% were imported and 7 % were imported-related, and 
597: together counting for 764 cases, which is significantly higher compared to 2023 (6.4%). Most imported infections 
598: were acquired from other European countries, either within the EU/EEA (26%) or non-EU/EEA regions (39%), 
599: followed by Asia (22%) and Africa (4%). Importations from Austria, Germany, Spain, France, Italy, and Romania 
600: collectively accounted for 65% of these cases. This notable increase in imported measles highlights the need and 
601: value of international collaboration, including timely information exchange to prevent further cross-border 
602: transmission and outbreaks within the EU/EEA region. In addition, checking and updating vaccination against 
603: measles should be a routine practice during travel medicine consultations and general health checks prior to 
604: travelling, including those travelling within the EU/EEA [13]. Strengthening exchange of information on crossborder cases via established EU and international channels is important to avoid re-establishment of measles in 
605: receiving countries.
606: 
607: All EU/EEA countries have adopted national, publicly funded childhood vaccination programmes targeting measles, 
608: mumps, and rubella (MMR). Among these, eleven countries — Bulgaria, Croatia, Czechia, France, Germany (under 
609: the Measles Protection Act), Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Poland, Slovakia, and Slovenia—have implemented mandatory 
610: MMR vaccination policies, primarily enforced through school-based mechanisms. France (2018), Germany (2019), 
611: and Italy (2017) recently introduced mandatory vaccination, with preliminary findings indicating increased 
612: vaccination coverage among targeted groups; however, additional analyses are necessary to evaluate the longterm impact and effectiveness of these interventions [14]. Typically, the first MMR dose is scheduled between 12–
613: 18 months of age, with earlier administration (9–11 months) recommended in Austria, Germany, Liechtenstein, 
614: and Slovenia. The timing of the second dose varies considerably across countries, ranging from early in the second 
615: year of life in Austria and Germany to preschool or primary school ages elsewhere. Additionally, catch-up 
616: recommendations vary widely, with Spain, for example, extending vaccination opportunities up to 64 years of age [15].
617: 
618: ---
619: 
620: Modelling studies suggest that in countries with substantial immunity gaps, supplementary immunisation strategies 
621: targeting individuals not covered by existing programmes may be required to achieve interruption of measles 
622: transmission [16].
623: 
624: The latest WHO estimates on national immunisation coverage for 2023 show a slight overall decrease in 
625: vaccination coverage within the EU/EEA compared to previous years; however, the estimates remained relatively 
626: consistent over the last five years. In 2023, the overall weighted vaccination coverage in the EU/EEA was 93.9% 
627: for the first dose (MCV1) and 88.8% for the second dose (MCV2). Six countries reported decreased coverage for 
628: the first measles vaccine dose, with Romania experiencing the most significant reduction (from 83% in 2022 to 
629: 78% in 2023). Similarly, nine countries reported decreased coverage for the second dose. While fifteen EU/EEA 
630: countries (50%) reached the ≥95% threshold for the first vaccine dose, only four countries (14%)—Hungary, 
631: Malta, Portugal, and Slovakia—achieved this threshold for the second dose. This represents a decline compared to 
632: the seven countries (Bulgaria, Hungary, Latvia, Malta, Norway, Portugal, and Slovakia) meeting the ≥95% 
633: benchmark for MCV2 in 2019, highlighting persistent challenges in attaining optimal vaccination coverage required 
634: for measles elimination. It is also to be noted that in two countries there was a positive upward trend of 3% or 
635: above (range up to 7%) when comparing the estimates from 2020 to 2023 for the first dose, and an upward trend 
636: in four countries for the second dose. A downward trend of 3% or more was observed in eight countries, both for 
637: the first and the second dose.
638: 
639: The European Regional Verification Commission for Measles and Rubella Elimination (RVC), which was established 
640: in 2011 [13] monitors the progress of the countries of the WHO European Region in relation to measles and rubella 
641: elimination. During the 12th RCV meeting, held in 2023, with reference to the data of 2022, it was concluded that 
642: 20 EU/EEA Member States provided evidence to demonstrate the elimination of endemic measles, whereas five 
643: countries were considered endemic, three countries were considered to have re-established measles transmission 
644: and for one country, the status is still pending [16].
645: 
646: ### Public health implications
647: 
648: ECDC continues to closely monitor measles activity in the EU/EEA, providing monthly epidemiological updates and 
649: assessments to support Member States' public health actions. ECDC continues to recommend the following actions 
650: for a public health response: closing immunity gaps through achieving and maintaining ≥95% vaccination coverage 
651: with two doses of measles-containing vaccine, enhancing surveillance quality, ensuring rapid detection, diagnosis, 
652: and outbreak control, and raising clinical awareness among healthcare providers. The deployment of upgraded 
653: digitalised immunisation information systems to identify and reach the unvaccinated is also critical and should form
654: an integral part of national efforts to improve the performance and management.
655: 
656: ### Conclusion
657: 
658: In 2024, the EU/EEA region recorded the highest number of measles cases observed in the past two decades, 
659: significantly exceeding pre-pandemic levels. This sharp increase underscores persistent immunity gaps and 
660: vulnerabilities within the population, exacerbated by suboptimal measles vaccination coverage. Although the 
661: impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on immunisation programmes varied by country — with some experiencing 
662: declines and others maintaining or slightly improving coverage — most EU/EEA countries have yet to achieve or 
663: sustain the ≥95% vaccination coverage target with two doses of measles-containing vaccine. Enhanced 
664: epidemiological surveillance, prompt outbreak investigation, and control measures remain critical for interrupting 
665: transmission and achieving regional elimination targets. Urgent action to address existing immunity gaps through 
666: targeted catch-up vaccination campaigns, particularly among populations disproportionately impacted by pandemic 
667: disruptions are essential. Strengthened public health communication and accelerated efforts to enhance vaccine 
668: acceptance remain crucial for restoring high immunisation coverage and preventing future measles outbreaks in 
669: the EU/EEA.

51: 
52: ### Introduction
53: 
54: Measles is an acute, highly contagious viral disease capable of causing epidemics. It is caused by a single-stranded 
55: ribonucleic acid (RNA) virus of the genus Morbillivirus and the family Paramyxoviridae. The virus is transmitted 
56: from person-to-person via respiratory droplets produced when infected people cough and sneeze. Virus-containing 
57: droplets can remain in the air for several hours, and the virus remains infectious on contaminated surfaces for up 
58: to two hours [1]. It is characterised by symptoms such as high fever, cough, runny nose, inflamed eyes, and a 
59: distinctive red rash that spreads across the body. Complications can be severe and include pneumonia, hearing 
60: loss, encephalitis, and death [1].
61: 
62: Measles is extremely infectious and it is estimated that 90% of non-immune people exposed to an individual with 
63: the infection will contract the disease. Mathematical models estimate the basic reproductive number at 12–18, i.e. 
64: the average number of secondary infections that follow a single introduction into a susceptible population.
65: Immunisation against measles started in the 1960s and has dramatically reduced the incidence of measles in 
66: Europe. But despite overall high immunisation coverage, measles continues to circulate. Globally, measles remains 
67: a leading cause of childhood death, and an estimated 140 000 children die each year from complications caused by 
68: the disease.
69: 
70: Measles prevention at the individual level requires two doses of a measles-containing vaccine (MCV). At population 
71: level, achieving and sustaining a vaccination coverage of at least 95% with two doses is essential to control the 
72: spread of the disease and prevent outbreaks. Immunisation remains the cornerstone of measles control and 
73: outbreak prevention [1, 2].
74: 
75: ### Methods
76: 
77: This report is based on data for 2024 retrieved from EpiPulse Cases on 20 March 2025. EpiPulse Cases is a newly 
78: introduced system for the collection, analysis and dissemination of data on communicable diseases that replaced 
79: The European Surveillance System (TESSy) in October 2024.
80: 
81: For a detailed description of methods used to produce this report, please refer to the ‘Methods’ chapter [3]. An 
82: overview of the national surveillance systems is available online [4].
83: 
84: A subset of the data used for this report is available through ECDC’s online ‘Surveillance atlas of infectious 
85: diseases’[5] and the Monthly Measles and Rubella Reports [6] where additional information may also be found in 
86: relation to surveillance systems and historical changes to surveillance, as well as possibility to download datasets
87: and additional visualisations.
88: 
89: ECDC has coordinated the surveillance of measles at the European level since the transfer of EUVAC.NET 
90: (European surveillance network for selected vaccine-preventable diseases, hosted by Statens Serum Institute, 
91: Denmark) to ECDC in 2011. Thirty European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA) Member States report 
92: measles data to ECDC. The 2008, 2012, or 2018 EU case definition [4, 7] are used by 27 countries and the 
93: majority report data from comprehensive, passive surveillance systems with national coverage. Belgium has
94: reported aggregated data since 2017, and Poland from (and including) April 2019. Up to December 2020, thirty 
95: countries (29 EU countries plus the UK) reported measles data on a routine basis. The United Kingdom (UK) 
96: stopped reporting measles cases to TESSy in December 2020<sup>1</sup>.
97: 
98: Data submitted by EU/EEA Member States are shared with the WHO Regional Office for Europe monthly as part of 
99: the measles surveillance of the WHO European Region. Vaccination coverage estimates presented in this report 
100: were obtained from the WHO Global Health Observatory website, WUENIC estimates [8]. The method of 
101: calculating MCV1 and MCV2 coverage are outlined in the metadata available for each indicator online [9].
102: 
103: ### Epidemiology
104: 
105: In the EU/EEA, measles activity began to increase in 2023 after a period of unusually low activity during 2020–
106: 2022, coinciding with the COVID-19 pandemic [2]. In 2024, a total of 35 212 cases of measles were reported 
107: across the EU/EEA, marking a notable increase from the 3 973 cases reported in 2023. All 28 EU/EEA countries 
108: reported measles activity in 2024, and two countries (Latvia and Liechtenstein) reported zero cases (Table 1, 
109: Figure 1). Romania accounted for the vast majority of reported cases (87%), with a total of 30 692 cases. The 
110: overall notification rate increased significantly in 2024 to 77.4 cases per 1 000 000 population, compared to 9.1 in 
111: 2023, 0.3 in 2022, 0.2 in 2021, and 4.6 in 2020, and it was also higher than the pre-pandemic rate in 2019 (27.2)
112: [10] (Table 1, Figure 1).
113: 
114: <sup>1</sup>The United Kingdom (UK) was a former Member State of the European Union (EU). The UK withdrew from the EU on 31 
115: January 2020, but continued reporting measles cases to TESSy till December 2020.
116:

118: 
119: Notification rates varied widely across EU/EEA countries, ranging from 0 in Latvia and Liechtenstein to a high of 
120: 1 610.7 cases per 1 000 000 population in Romania. Other countries reporting high notification rates included 
121: Austria (59.5 cases per 1 000 000), Belgium (44.9), and Ireland (39.6). (Table 1, Figure 2)
122: 
123: The number of cases reported in 2024 are the highest reported in the previous five years. This number also
124: exceeded the total number of cases reported in 2019 (pre COVID-19), which was 12 320 cases [10].

234: #### Seasonality and trend
235: 
236: In 2024, measles epidemiology returned to its typical seasonal pattern within the EU/EEA, with the highest number 
237: of cases reported from February to July, followed by a gradual decline during the second half of the year (Figure 
238: 3). This contrasts with 2023, when measles activity did not follow the usual seasonality pattern and instead 
239: increased predominantly in the latter half of the year, diverging from the expected epidemiological trend. The 
240: marked resurgence in 2024 emphasises a return to more typical measles seasonal patterns, but at significantly 
241: elevated levels compared to the pandemic and pre-pandemic years (Figure 4).

286: #### Age distribution:
287: 
288: In 2024, of the 35 212 measles cases reported, infants under one year of age remained the most affected group, 
289: with a notably high notification rate of 1 175.4 cases per 1 000 000 population (13%). The next most affected 
290: groups were children aged 1–4 years with a notification rate of 688.7 cases per 1 000 000 (33.1%), followed by 
291: children aged 5–9 years with a rate of 247.1 cases per 1 000 000 (16%). The rates progressively decreased with 
292: age, recording 169.9 per 1 000 000 among 10–14-year-olds (11.6%), 129.4 per 1 000 000 in the 15–19 age group
293: (8.8%), 45.8 per 1 000 000 among young adults aged 20–29 years (6.5%), and 12.2 per 1 000 000 in individuals 
294: aged 30 years and older (10.9%) (Figure 5). Overall, 26.3% of cases were above 14 years of age and 46.1% were 
295: below the age of five years which highlights the fact that measles affects all age groups.
296: 
297: The median age of cases across all EU/EEA countries that submitted age-based data in 2024 was five years of age 
298: (interquartile range, IQR:2-15), corresponding to 2023, where the median age was 5 as well, while the IQR was 2-
299: 12. In 2024, as was the case in 2023, the overall age distribution of cases was heavily influenced by the high 
300: number of cases in Romania. In Romania the majority of cases were reported among the 1-4 years old age group
301: accounting for 35.5% of the total cases. In contrast, in several EU/EEA countries the majority of cases reported
302: were among the +30-age group (France: 28.4%, Poland: 34.4%, Spain: 38.5%, Italy: 52.4%).

320: ### Vaccination status
321: 
322: Data on vaccination status were available for 31 804 cases (90%) reported in 2024. Of these cases, 27 692 (87%) 
323: were unvaccinated, 2 692 (8%) were vaccinated with one dose of measles-containing vaccine, 1 374 (4%) were 
324: vaccinated with two or more doses, and 46 cases (0.1%) were vaccinated with an unknown number of doses 
325: (Figure 6). The proportion of reported unvaccinated cases for 2024 was the highest observed in the last five years.
326: 
327: Among cases with known vaccination status, the highest proportion of unvaccinated cases by age group was those 
328: aged <1 year (98%), a group not routinely targeted with measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccination in most 
329: countries, followed by those aged 1–4 years (90%), 5–9 years (84%), and 10-14 years (80%), 15-19 years (78%), 
330: 20-29 years (83%), and for +30 years (87%). Vaccination status was more likely to be unknown with increasing 
331: age, accounting for 28% and 24% of cases aged 30+ years and 20–29 years, respectively.
332:

334: 
335: For the years 2019–2023, the overall distribution of cases by age group and vaccination status followed the same 
336: pattern, with the unvaccinated population of 0–9 years and >20 years of age counting for approximately 80% of 
337: the total number of cases (Figure 7).
338: 
339: The proportion of children aged 1–4 years who were unvaccinated in 2024 (90%) remained equally high compared 
340: to 2023 (88%) and to what was observed in the period 2019–2022, when 80% of children of this age group were 
341: unvaccinated and 98% of children aged <1 year were unvaccinated.
342: 
343: When vaccination status was known and in relation to younger adults (>14 years) and adults >20 years, the 
344: majority were not vaccinated or not fully vaccinated (82% and 85% respectively unvaccinated, and 9% and 7%
345: respectively vaccinated only with one dose).

379: #### Vaccination coverage
380: 
381: Data on vaccination coverage for the first and second dose of measles-containing vaccine were available up to 
382: 2023. In 2023, the overall population weighted vaccination coverage for the EU/EEA countries was 93.9% for the 
383: first dose and 88.8% for the second dose, which represents a slight decrease compared to previous years (Table 
384: 2). Six countries reported a decrease in the vaccination coverage for the first dose of measles in 2023 compared to 
385: the coverage reported in 2022, (the highest decrease was reported in Romania (83% in 2022, and 78 in 2023))
386: and an additional nine countries reported a decrease in coverage for the second dose. Moreover, three countries 
387: reported an increase in vaccination coverage for dose one (range 1-2%) and four countries for dose two (1-3%). 
388: Fifteen countries (50%) reported a coverage of ≥95% for dose one and only four countries (14%) (Hungary, 
389: Malta, Portugal, and Slovakia) had a coverage of ≥95% for the second dose (Figure 8, Figure 9). Only three
390: countries had an estimated coverage of ≥95% for both MCV1 and MCV2 in 2023 (Hungary, Malta, and Portugal).
391: 
392: The percent of change in vaccination coverage between 2020 and 2023 showed some variation. While Austria 
393: demonstrated the largest percentage of improvement for the second dose (+6%), Romania experienced the 
394: sharpest decline in both doses (–9% for dose one, –13% for dose two). A total of 16 countries showed a decrease 
395: in coverage for at least one dose, with declines more pronounced for dose two. The overall EU/EEA vaccination 
396: coverage average dropped slightly by 0.5% for MCV1 and 0.8% for MCV2 in 2023 compared to 2020. (Table 2)
397: 
398: #### Outcome
399: 
400: In 2024, the disease outcome was reported for 31 430 cases (89% of total cases). There were 23 deaths 
401: attributable to measles, which was a significant increase compared to previous years. Romania reported the 
402: majority of these deaths (22 deaths), with one additional death reported from Ireland. In comparison, three deaths 
403: were reported in 2023 retrospectively, and no deaths were reported in the preceding two years (2021–2022), while 
404: two deaths occurred in 2020 and ten deaths were recorded in 2019 in EU/EEA countries. This highlights a 
405: resurgence in severe measles outcomes in 2024.
406: 
407: When considering the age of the deaths, five cases were in children <1 year old, nine deaths in children between 
408: 1-4 years, two deaths in adults between 20-29 years, and seven deaths in the age group over 30 years of age. 
409: Sixteen of those who died where unvaccinated, five had only one dose, and two people had unknown vaccination status.
410: 
411: #### Hospitalisation and complications
412: 
413: Hospitalisation status was available for 31 035 (88%) cases, of which 24 529 (79%) were hospitalised in 2024. 
414: Among the hospitalised cases, 20 095 (82%) were unvaccinated. 1 809 (7%) individuals had received one dose of 
415: measles-containing vaccine, 739 (3%) individuals had received two or more doses, and 1 886 (8%) individuals had 
416: unknown vaccination status. The most hospitalised cases (96%) were reported by Romania. The median age of 
417: hospitalised cases reported in the EU/EEA was five years (IQR: 2-15 years).
418: 
419: Among all reported cases in 2024, data on complications were reported for 24 239 (68%) cases, 1 483 of which 
420: (6%) had no complications. Reported complications included 6 769 (28%) cases of pneumonia, 187 cases of 
421: diarrhoea, 19 cases of otitis media and 10 cases of acute encephalitis. Unspecified complications (‘other’) were 
422: reported for 15 744 (64.9%) cases. Of these 24 239 cases reported with complications, 19 420 (80%) cases were 
423: unvaccinated. The median age of the cases presented with complications was five years (IQR: 2–15 years).
424: 
425: #### Importations
426: 
427: In 2024, importation status was available for 2 866 (8%) cases. Of these cases, 542 (18%) were classified as 
428: imported in 2024 and 222 as import-related (7%) meaning the source of infection (exposure) was outside the 
429: reporting country. Twenty-six countries reported imported measles cases for 2024, the majority of which were 
430: reported by Austria (44), Germany (81), Spain (54), France (86), Italy (52), and Romania (39), accounting for 65% 
431: of all imported cases. The median age of these cases was five years (range 0–91 years).
432: 
433: Among the 542 imported cases for which a single probable country of infection was available, most individuals
434: were thought to have acquired their infection in Europe (EU/EEA: 26%, non-EU/EEA: 39%), followed by Asia 
435: (22%), and Africa (4%). An unknown origin of infection was reported for 8% of the cases. Of the 68 different 
436: countries listed as the likely origin of infection of imported cases, five countries accounted for 50% of these 
437: infections: Romania (122), Morocco (53), UK (36), Bosnia and Herzegovina (35), and Italy (25).
438: 
439: The proportion of imported measles cases for 2024 appeared to be higher than 2023 and 2022; 128 (5%) cases 
440: and 22 (18%) cases respectively, and higher than the pre-pandemic period as well, which was 62 (3%) cases in 
441: 2020, 644 (5%) cases in 2019.

555: ### Discussion
556: 
557: There was a significant escalation in measles transmission in 2024 compared to previous years, highlighted by the 
558: epidemiological data presented above. A total of 35 212 measles cases were reported, resulting in an overall 
559: notification rate of 77.4 cases per 1 000 000 population — a significant increase compared to the 2023 rate of 5.3 
560: per 1 000 000 population. Romania continued to report the highest notification rate, with 1 610.7 cases per 
561: 1 000 000 population, substantially higher than its 2023 rate (92.2 cases per 1 000 000).
562: 
563: The first half of 2024 showed a particularly sharp increase in measles activity, reaching levels higher than any level 
564: recorded over the past two decades, before it declined again toward the end of the year. In response to this rapid 
565: rise in cases, ECDC issued a dedicated Threat Assessment Brief emphasising the ongoing public health risk, 
566: highlighting concerns around sub-optimal vaccination coverage, the high potential for cross-border transmission, 
567: and the anticipated seasonal peak which further compounded the risk [2].
568: 
569: Similar to previous years, measles continued to affect individuals across all age groups in 2024. Infants under one 
570: year of age were the most severely impacted, showing the highest incidence at 1 175.4 cases per 1 000 000 
571: population. This population group remains particularly vulnerable since infants under one year are typically too 
572: young for direct vaccination and thus rely heavily on population immunity for protection. In 2024, 87% of all cases 
573: with known vaccination status were unvaccinated. Among children aged one to four years, who would typically 
574: receive their first dose of measles vaccine in national vaccination schedules, the rate remained high at 688.7 per 
575: 1 000 000 population, with 90% of these children unvaccinated, underlying the fact that ongoing gaps are present 
576: in this critical age group.
577: 
578: The age distribution of measles cases in 2024 reveals a notable difference between the EU/EEA countries. In 
579: Romania, over one-third of all cases were in children aged 1–4 years, while in several other countries (e.g. Italy, 
580: Spain, France, Poland), the majority of cases occurred in adults aged 30 years and older. This difference may
581: indicate variation in vaccination coverage in the age groups over a longer historical period and the gaps in catch-up 
582: vaccination strategies. Romania’s sharp drop in MCV1 and MCV2 coverage over recent years, especially among 
583: young children, likely facilitated early-age transmission [11]. Conversely, in countries with higher current childhood 
584: coverage but missed vaccinations in the past, older cohorts are now more exposed and at risk of infection [12].
585: 
586: Hospitalisation rates for measles cases remained consistently high in 2024, with 79% of reported cases required
587: hospitalisation. This aligns closely with the 2023 hospitalisation rate of 80% but significantly exceeds earlier figures 
588: from preceding years (33% in 2022 and 55% in 2019). Additionally, most hospitalised individuals—approximately 
589: 85% — were unvaccinated. In 2024, complications from measles were frequently reported, predominantly 
590: affecting unvaccinated individuals. Among hospitalised patients, complications such as pneumonia, otitis media, 
591: and encephalitis continued to be prevalent. Importantly, 2024 recorded 23 measles-related deaths (of which 22 
592: were reported from Romania), a marked increase compared to the three fatalities reported in 2023. Notably, 14 
593: deaths were reported in children below the age of five years.
594: 
595: While the majority of measles cases reported in 2024 originated from local transmission within EU/EEA countries, 
596: among the cases with known importation status, 18% were imported and 7 % were imported-related, and 
597: together counting for 764 cases, which is significantly higher compared to 2023 (6.4%). Most imported infections 
598: were acquired from other European countries, either within the EU/EEA (26%) or non-EU/EEA regions (39%), 
599: followed by Asia (22%) and Africa (4%). Importations from Austria, Germany, Spain, France, Italy, and Romania 
600: collectively accounted for 65% of these cases. This notable increase in imported measles highlights the need and 
601: value of international collaboration, including timely information exchange to prevent further cross-border 
602: transmission and outbreaks within the EU/EEA region. In addition, checking and updating vaccination against 
603: measles should be a routine practice during travel medicine consultations and general health checks prior to 
604: travelling, including those travelling within the EU/EEA [13]. Strengthening exchange of information on crossborder cases via established EU and international channels is important to avoid re-establishment of measles in 
605: receiving countries.
606: 
607: All EU/EEA countries have adopted national, publicly funded childhood vaccination programmes targeting measles, 
608: mumps, and rubella (MMR). Among these, eleven countries — Bulgaria, Croatia, Czechia, France, Germany (under 
609: the Measles Protection Act), Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Poland, Slovakia, and Slovenia—have implemented mandatory 
610: MMR vaccination policies, primarily enforced through school-based mechanisms. France (2018), Germany (2019), 
611: and Italy (2017) recently introduced mandatory vaccination, with preliminary findings indicating increased 
612: vaccination coverage among targeted groups; however, additional analyses are necessary to evaluate the longterm impact and effectiveness of these interventions [14]. Typically, the first MMR dose is scheduled between 12–
613: 18 months of age, with earlier administration (9–11 months) recommended in Austria, Germany, Liechtenstein, 
614: and Slovenia. The timing of the second dose varies considerably across countries, ranging from early in the second 
615: year of life in Austria and Germany to preschool or primary school ages elsewhere. Additionally, catch-up 
616: recommendations vary widely, with Spain, for example, extending vaccination opportunities up to 64 years of age [15].
617: 
618: ---
619: 
620: Modelling studies suggest that in countries with substantial immunity gaps, supplementary immunisation strategies 
621: targeting individuals not covered by existing programmes may be required to achieve interruption of measles 
622: transmission [16].
623: 
624: The latest WHO estimates on national immunisation coverage for 2023 show a slight overall decrease in 
625: vaccination coverage within the EU/EEA compared to previous years; however, the estimates remained relatively 
626: consistent over the last five years. In 2023, the overall weighted vaccination coverage in the EU/EEA was 93.9% 
627: for the first dose (MCV1) and 88.8% for the second dose (MCV2). Six countries reported decreased coverage for 
628: the first measles vaccine dose, with Romania experiencing the most significant reduction (from 83% in 2022 to 
629: 78% in 2023). Similarly, nine countries reported decreased coverage for the second dose. While fifteen EU/EEA 
630: countries (50%) reached the ≥95% threshold for the first vaccine dose, only four countries (14%)—Hungary, 
631: Malta, Portugal, and Slovakia—achieved this threshold for the second dose. This represents a decline compared to 
632: the seven countries (Bulgaria, Hungary, Latvia, Malta, Norway, Portugal, and Slovakia) meeting the ≥95% 
633: benchmark for MCV2 in 2019, highlighting persistent challenges in attaining optimal vaccination coverage required 
634: for measles elimination. It is also to be noted that in two countries there was a positive upward trend of 3% or 
635: above (range up to 7%) when comparing the estimates from 2020 to 2023 for the first dose, and an upward trend 
636: in four countries for the second dose. A downward trend of 3% or more was observed in eight countries, both for 
637: the first and the second dose.
638: 
639: The European Regional Verification Commission for Measles and Rubella Elimination (RVC), which was established 
640: in 2011 [13] monitors the progress of the countries of the WHO European Region in relation to measles and rubella 
641: elimination. During the 12th RCV meeting, held in 2023, with reference to the data of 2022, it was concluded that 
642: 20 EU/EEA Member States provided evidence to demonstrate the elimination of endemic measles, whereas five 
643: countries were considered endemic, three countries were considered to have re-established measles transmission 
644: and for one country, the status is still pending [16].
645: 
646: ### Public health implications
647: 
648: ECDC continues to closely monitor measles activity in the EU/EEA, providing monthly epidemiological updates and 
649: assessments to support Member States' public health actions. ECDC continues to recommend the following actions 
650: for a public health response: closing immunity gaps through achieving and maintaining ≥95% vaccination coverage 
651: with two doses of measles-containing vaccine, enhancing surveillance quality, ensuring rapid detection, diagnosis, 
652: and outbreak control, and raising clinical awareness among healthcare providers. The deployment of upgraded 
653: digitalised immunisation information systems to identify and reach the unvaccinated is also critical and should form
654: an integral part of national efforts to improve the performance and management.
655: 
656: ### Conclusion
657: 
658: In 2024, the EU/EEA region recorded the highest number of measles cases observed in the past two decades, 
659: significantly exceeding pre-pandemic levels. This sharp increase underscores persistent immunity gaps and 
660: vulnerabilities within the population, exacerbated by suboptimal measles vaccination coverage. Although the 
661: impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on immunisation programmes varied by country — with some experiencing 
662: declines and others maintaining or slightly improving coverage — most EU/EEA countries have yet to achieve or 
663: sustain the ≥95% vaccination coverage target with two doses of measles-containing vaccine. Enhanced 
664: epidemiological surveillance, prompt outbreak investigation, and control measures remain critical for interrupting 
665: transmission and achieving regional elimination targets. Urgent action to address existing immunity gaps through 
666: targeted catch-up vaccination campaigns, particularly among populations disproportionately impacted by pandemic 
667: disruptions are essential. Strengthened public health communication and accelerated efforts to enhance vaccine 
668: acceptance remain crucial for restoring high immunisation coverage and preventing future measles outbreaks in 
669: the EU/EEA.

51: 
52: ### Introduction
53: 
54: Measles is an acute, highly contagious viral disease capable of causing epidemics. It is caused by a single-stranded 
55: ribonucleic acid (RNA) virus of the genus Morbillivirus and the family Paramyxoviridae. The virus is transmitted 
56: from person-to-person via respiratory droplets produced when infected people cough and sneeze. Virus-containing 
57: droplets can remain in the air for several hours, and the virus remains infectious on contaminated surfaces for up 
58: to two hours [1]. It is characterised by symptoms such as high fever, cough, runny nose, inflamed eyes, and a 
59: distinctive red rash that spreads across the body. Complications can be severe and include pneumonia, hearing 
60: loss, encephalitis, and death [1].
61: 
62: Measles is extremely infectious and it is estimated that 90% of non-immune people exposed to an individual with 
63: the infection will contract the disease. Mathematical models estimate the basic reproductive number at 12–18, i.e. 
64: the average number of secondary infections that follow a single introduction into a susceptible population.
65: Immunisation against measles started in the 1960s and has dramatically reduced the incidence of measles in 
66: Europe. But despite overall high immunisation coverage, measles continues to circulate. Globally, measles remains 
67: a leading cause of childhood death, and an estimated 140 000 children die each year from complications caused by 
68: the disease.
69: 
70: Measles prevention at the individual level requires two doses of a measles-containing vaccine (MCV). At population 
71: level, achieving and sustaining a vaccination coverage of at least 95% with two doses is essential to control the 
72: spread of the disease and prevent outbreaks. Immunisation remains the cornerstone of measles control and 
73: outbreak prevention [1, 2].
74: 
75: ### Methods
76: 
77: This report is based on data for 2024 retrieved from EpiPulse Cases on 20 March 2025. EpiPulse Cases is a newly 
78: introduced system for the collection, analysis and dissemination of data on communicable diseases that replaced 
79: The European Surveillance System (TESSy) in October 2024.
80: 
81: For a detailed description of methods used to produce this report, please refer to the ‘Methods’ chapter [3]. An 
82: overview of the national surveillance systems is available online [4].
83: 
84: A subset of the data used for this report is available through ECDC’s online ‘Surveillance atlas of infectious 
85: diseases’[5] and the Monthly Measles and Rubella Reports [6] where additional information may also be found in 
86: relation to surveillance systems and historical changes to surveillance, as well as possibility to download datasets
87: and additional visualisations.
88: 
89: ECDC has coordinated the surveillance of measles at the European level since the transfer of EUVAC.NET 
90: (European surveillance network for selected vaccine-preventable diseases, hosted by Statens Serum Institute, 
91: Denmark) to ECDC in 2011. Thirty European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA) Member States report 
92: measles data to ECDC. The 2008, 2012, or 2018 EU case definition [4, 7] are used by 27 countries and the 
93: majority report data from comprehensive, passive surveillance systems with national coverage. Belgium has
94: reported aggregated data since 2017, and Poland from (and including) April 2019. Up to December 2020, thirty 
95: countries (29 EU countries plus the UK) reported measles data on a routine basis. The United Kingdom (UK) 
96: stopped reporting measles cases to TESSy in December 2020<sup>1</sup>.
97: 
98: Data submitted by EU/EEA Member States are shared with the WHO Regional Office for Europe monthly as part of 
99: the measles surveillance of the WHO European Region. Vaccination coverage estimates presented in this report 
100: were obtained from the WHO Global Health Observatory website, WUENIC estimates [8]. The method of 
101: calculating MCV1 and MCV2 coverage are outlined in the metadata available for each indicator online [9].
102: 
103: ### Epidemiology
104: 
105: In the EU/EEA, measles activity began to increase in 2023 after a period of unusually low activity during 2020–
106: 2022, coinciding with the COVID-19 pandemic [2]. In 2024, a total of 35 212 cases of measles were reported 
107: across the EU/EEA, marking a notable increase from the 3 973 cases reported in 2023. All 28 EU/EEA countries 
108: reported measles activity in 2024, and two countries (Latvia and Liechtenstein) reported zero cases (Table 1, 
109: Figure 1). Romania accounted for the vast majority of reported cases (87%), with a total of 30 692 cases. The 
110: overall notification rate increased significantly in 2024 to 77.4 cases per 1 000 000 population, compared to 9.1 in 
111: 2023, 0.3 in 2022, 0.2 in 2021, and 4.6 in 2020, and it was also higher than the pre-pandemic rate in 2019 (27.2)
112: [10] (Table 1, Figure 1).
113: 
114: <sup>1</sup>The United Kingdom (UK) was a former Member State of the European Union (EU). The UK withdrew from the EU on 31 
115: January 2020, but continued reporting measles cases to TESSy till December 2020.
116:

118: 
119: Notification rates varied widely across EU/EEA countries, ranging from 0 in Latvia and Liechtenstein to a high of 
120: 1 610.7 cases per 1 000 000 population in Romania. Other countries reporting high notification rates included 
121: Austria (59.5 cases per 1 000 000), Belgium (44.9), and Ireland (39.6). (Table 1, Figure 2)
122: 
123: The number of cases reported in 2024 are the highest reported in the previous five years. This number also
124: exceeded the total number of cases reported in 2019 (pre COVID-19), which was 12 320 cases [10].

234: #### Seasonality and trend
235: 
236: In 2024, measles epidemiology returned to its typical seasonal pattern within the EU/EEA, with the highest number 
237: of cases reported from February to July, followed by a gradual decline during the second half of the year (Figure 
238: 3). This contrasts with 2023, when measles activity did not follow the usual seasonality pattern and instead 
239: increased predominantly in the latter half of the year, diverging from the expected epidemiological trend. The 
240: marked resurgence in 2024 emphasises a return to more typical measles seasonal patterns, but at significantly 
241: elevated levels compared to the pandemic and pre-pandemic years (Figure 4).

286: #### Age distribution:
287: 
288: In 2024, of the 35 212 measles cases reported, infants under one year of age remained the most affected group, 
289: with a notably high notification rate of 1 175.4 cases per 1 000 000 population (13%). The next most affected 
290: groups were children aged 1–4 years with a notification rate of 688.7 cases per 1 000 000 (33.1%), followed by 
291: children aged 5–9 years with a rate of 247.1 cases per 1 000 000 (16%). The rates progressively decreased with 
292: age, recording 169.9 per 1 000 000 among 10–14-year-olds (11.6%), 129.4 per 1 000 000 in the 15–19 age group
293: (8.8%), 45.8 per 1 000 000 among young adults aged 20–29 years (6.5%), and 12.2 per 1 000 000 in individuals 
294: aged 30 years and older (10.9%) (Figure 5). Overall, 26.3% of cases were above 14 years of age and 46.1% were 
295: below the age of five years which highlights the fact that measles affects all age groups.
296: 
297: The median age of cases across all EU/EEA countries that submitted age-based data in 2024 was five years of age 
298: (interquartile range, IQR:2-15), corresponding to 2023, where the median age was 5 as well, while the IQR was 2-
299: 12. In 2024, as was the case in 2023, the overall age distribution of cases was heavily influenced by the high 
300: number of cases in Romania. In Romania the majority of cases were reported among the 1-4 years old age group
301: accounting for 35.5% of the total cases. In contrast, in several EU/EEA countries the majority of cases reported
302: were among the +30-age group (France: 28.4%, Poland: 34.4%, Spain: 38.5%, Italy: 52.4%).

320: ### Vaccination status
321: 
322: Data on vaccination status were available for 31 804 cases (90%) reported in 2024. Of these cases, 27 692 (87%) 
323: were unvaccinated, 2 692 (8%) were vaccinated with one dose of measles-containing vaccine, 1 374 (4%) were 
324: vaccinated with two or more doses, and 46 cases (0.1%) were vaccinated with an unknown number of doses 
325: (Figure 6). The proportion of reported unvaccinated cases for 2024 was the highest observed in the last five years.
326: 
327: Among cases with known vaccination status, the highest proportion of unvaccinated cases by age group was those 
328: aged <1 year (98%), a group not routinely targeted with measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccination in most 
329: countries, followed by those aged 1–4 years (90%), 5–9 years (84%), and 10-14 years (80%), 15-19 years (78%), 
330: 20-29 years (83%), and for +30 years (87%). Vaccination status was more likely to be unknown with increasing 
331: age, accounting for 28% and 24% of cases aged 30+ years and 20–29 years, respectively.
332: 
333: ---
334: 
335: For the years 2019–2023, the overall distribution of cases by age group and vaccination status followed the same 
336: pattern, with the unvaccinated population of 0–9 years and >20 years of age counting for approximately 80% of 
337: the total number of cases (Figure 7).
338: 
339: The proportion of children aged 1–4 years who were unvaccinated in 2024 (90%) remained equally high compared 
340: to 2023 (88%) and to what was observed in the period 2019–2022, when 80% of children of this age group were 
341: unvaccinated and 98% of children aged <1 year were unvaccinated.
342: 
343: When vaccination status was known and in relation to younger adults (>14 years) and adults >20 years, the 
344: majority were not vaccinated or not fully vaccinated (82% and 85% respectively unvaccinated, and 9% and 7%
345: respectively vaccinated only with one dose).

379: #### Vaccination coverage
380: 
381: Data on vaccination coverage for the first and second dose of measles-containing vaccine were available up to 
382: 2023. In 2023, the overall population weighted vaccination coverage for the EU/EEA countries was 93.9% for the 
383: first dose and 88.8% for the second dose, which represents a slight decrease compared to previous years (Table 
384: 2). Six countries reported a decrease in the vaccination coverage for the first dose of measles in 2023 compared to 
385: the coverage reported in 2022, (the highest decrease was reported in Romania (83% in 2022, and 78 in 2023))
386: and an additional nine countries reported a decrease in coverage for the second dose. Moreover, three countries 
387: reported an increase in vaccination coverage for dose one (range 1-2%) and four countries for dose two (1-3%). 
388: Fifteen countries (50%) reported a coverage of ≥95% for dose one and only four countries (14%) (Hungary, 
389: Malta, Portugal, and Slovakia) had a coverage of ≥95% for the second dose (Figure 8, Figure 9). Only three
390: countries had an estimated coverage of ≥95% for both MCV1 and MCV2 in 2023 (Hungary, Malta, and Portugal).
391: 
392: The percent of change in vaccination coverage between 2020 and 2023 showed some variation. While Austria 
393: demonstrated the largest percentage of improvement for the second dose (+6%), Romania experienced the 
394: sharpest decline in both doses (–9% for dose one, –13% for dose two). A total of 16 countries showed a decrease 
395: in coverage for at least one dose, with declines more pronounced for dose two. The overall EU/EEA vaccination 
396: coverage average dropped slightly by 0.5% for MCV1 and 0.8% for MCV2 in 2023 compared to 2020. (Table 2)
397: 
398: #### Outcome
399: 
400: In 2024, the disease outcome was reported for 31 430 cases (89% of total cases). There were 23 deaths 
401: attributable to measles, which was a significant increase compared to previous years. Romania reported the 
402: majority of these deaths (22 deaths), with one additional death reported from Ireland. In comparison, three deaths 
403: were reported in 2023 retrospectively, and no deaths were reported in the preceding two years (2021–2022), while 
404: two deaths occurred in 2020 and ten deaths were recorded in 2019 in EU/EEA countries. This highlights a 
405: resurgence in severe measles outcomes in 2024.
406: 
407: When considering the age of the deaths, five cases were in children <1 year old, nine deaths in children between 
408: 1-4 years, two deaths in adults between 20-29 years, and seven deaths in the age group over 30 years of age. 
409: Sixteen of those who died where unvaccinated, five had only one dose, and two people had unknown vaccination status.
410: 
411: #### Hospitalisation and complications
412: 
413: Hospitalisation status was available for 31 035 (88%) cases, of which 24 529 (79%) were hospitalised in 2024. 
414: Among the hospitalised cases, 20 095 (82%) were unvaccinated. 1 809 (7%) individuals had received one dose of 
415: measles-containing vaccine, 739 (3%) individuals had received two or more doses, and 1 886 (8%) individuals had 
416: unknown vaccination status. The most hospitalised cases (96%) were reported by Romania. The median age of 
417: hospitalised cases reported in the EU/EEA was five years (IQR: 2-15 years).
418: 
419: Among all reported cases in 2024, data on complications were reported for 24 239 (68%) cases, 1 483 of which 
420: (6%) had no complications. Reported complications included 6 769 (28%) cases of pneumonia, 187 cases of 
421: diarrhoea, 19 cases of otitis media and 10 cases of acute encephalitis. Unspecified complications (‘other’) were 
422: reported for 15 744 (64.9%) cases. Of these 24 239 cases reported with complications, 19 420 (80%) cases were 
423: unvaccinated. The median age of the cases presented with complications was five years (IQR: 2–15 years).
424: 
425: #### Importations
426: 
427: In 2024, importation status was available for 2 866 (8%) cases. Of these cases, 542 (18%) were classified as 
428: imported in 2024 and 222 as import-related (7%) meaning the source of infection (exposure) was outside the 
429: reporting country. Twenty-six countries reported imported measles cases for 2024, the majority of which were 
430: reported by Austria (44), Germany (81), Spain (54), France (86), Italy (52), and Romania (39), accounting for 65% 
431: of all imported cases. The median age of these cases was five years (range 0–91 years).
432: 
433: Among the 542 imported cases for which a single probable country of infection was available, most individuals
434: were thought to have acquired their infection in Europe (EU/EEA: 26%, non-EU/EEA: 39%), followed by Asia 
435: (22%), and Africa (4%). An unknown origin of infection was reported for 8% of the cases. Of the 68 different 
436: countries listed as the likely origin of infection of imported cases, five countries accounted for 50% of these 
437: infections: Romania (122), Morocco (53), UK (36), Bosnia and Herzegovina (35), and Italy (25).
438: 
439: The proportion of imported measles cases for 2024 appeared to be higher than 2023 and 2022; 128 (5%) cases 
440: and 22 (18%) cases respectively, and higher than the pre-pandemic period as well, which was 62 (3%) cases in 
441: 2020, 644 (5%) cases in 2019.

555: ### Discussion
556: 
557: There was a significant escalation in measles transmission in 2024 compared to previous years, highlighted by the 
558: epidemiological data presented above. A total of 35 212 measles cases were reported, resulting in an overall 
559: notification rate of 77.4 cases per 1 000 000 population — a significant increase compared to the 2023 rate of 5.3 
560: per 1 000 000 population. Romania continued to report the highest notification rate, with 1 610.7 cases per 
561: 1 000 000 population, substantially higher than its 2023 rate (92.2 cases per 1 000 000).
562: 
563: The first half of 2024 showed a particularly sharp increase in measles activity, reaching levels higher than any level 
564: recorded over the past two decades, before it declined again toward the end of the year. In response to this rapid 
565: rise in cases, ECDC issued a dedicated Threat Assessment Brief emphasising the ongoing public health risk, 
566: highlighting concerns around sub-optimal vaccination coverage, the high potential for cross-border transmission, 
567: and the anticipated seasonal peak which further compounded the risk [2].
568: 
569: Similar to previous years, measles continued to affect individuals across all age groups in 2024. Infants under one 
570: year of age were the most severely impacted, showing the highest incidence at 1 175.4 cases per 1 000 000 
571: population. This population group remains particularly vulnerable since infants under one year are typically too 
572: young for direct vaccination and thus rely heavily on population immunity for protection. In 2024, 87% of all cases 
573: with known vaccination status were unvaccinated. Among children aged one to four years, who would typically 
574: receive their first dose of measles vaccine in national vaccination schedules, the rate remained high at 688.7 per 
575: 1 000 000 population, with 90% of these children unvaccinated, underlying the fact that ongoing gaps are present 
576: in this critical age group.
577: 
578: The age distribution of measles cases in 2024 reveals a notable difference between the EU/EEA countries. In 
579: Romania, over one-third of all cases were in children aged 1–4 years, while in several other countries (e.g. Italy, 
580: Spain, France, Poland), the majority of cases occurred in adults aged 30 years and older. This difference may
581: indicate variation in vaccination coverage in the age groups over a longer historical period and the gaps in catch-up 
582: vaccination strategies. Romania’s sharp drop in MCV1 and MCV2 coverage over recent years, especially among 
583: young children, likely facilitated early-age transmission [11]. Conversely, in countries with higher current childhood 
584: coverage but missed vaccinations in the past, older cohorts are now more exposed and at risk of infection [12].
585: 
586: Hospitalisation rates for measles cases remained consistently high in 2024, with 79% of reported cases required
587: hospitalisation. This aligns closely with the 2023 hospitalisation rate of 80% but significantly exceeds earlier figures 
588: from preceding years (33% in 2022 and 55% in 2019). Additionally, most hospitalised individuals—approximately 
589: 85% — were unvaccinated. In 2024, complications from measles were frequently reported, predominantly 
590: affecting unvaccinated individuals. Among hospitalised patients, complications such as pneumonia, otitis media, 
591: and encephalitis continued to be prevalent. Importantly, 2024 recorded 23 measles-related deaths (of which 22 
592: were reported from Romania), a marked increase compared to the three fatalities reported in 2023. Notably, 14 
593: deaths were reported in children below the age of five years.
594: 
595: While the majority of measles cases reported in 2024 originated from local transmission within EU/EEA countries, 
596: among the cases with known importation status, 18% were imported and 7 % were imported-related, and 
597: together counting for 764 cases, which is significantly higher compared to 2023 (6.4%). Most imported infections 
598: were acquired from other European countries, either within the EU/EEA (26%) or non-EU/EEA regions (39%), 
599: followed by Asia (22%) and Africa (4%). Importations from Austria, Germany, Spain, France, Italy, and Romania 
600: collectively accounted for 65% of these cases. This notable increase in imported measles highlights the need and 
601: value of international collaboration, including timely information exchange to prevent further cross-border 
602: transmission and outbreaks within the EU/EEA region. In addition, checking and updating vaccination against 
603: measles should be a routine practice during travel medicine consultations and general health checks prior to 
604: travelling, including those travelling within the EU/EEA [13]. Strengthening exchange of information on crossborder cases via established EU and international channels is important to avoid re-establishment of measles in 
605: receiving countries.
606: 
607: All EU/EEA countries have adopted national, publicly funded childhood vaccination programmes targeting measles, 
608: mumps, and rubella (MMR). Among these, eleven countries — Bulgaria, Croatia, Czechia, France, Germany (under 
609: the Measles Protection Act), Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Poland, Slovakia, and Slovenia—have implemented mandatory 
610: MMR vaccination policies, primarily enforced through school-based mechanisms. France (2018), Germany (2019), 
611: and Italy (2017) recently introduced mandatory vaccination, with preliminary findings indicating increased 
612: vaccination coverage among targeted groups; however, additional analyses are necessary to evaluate the longterm impact and effectiveness of these interventions [14]. Typically, the first MMR dose is scheduled between 12–
613: 18 months of age, with earlier administration (9–11 months) recommended in Austria, Germany, Liechtenstein, 
614: and Slovenia. The timing of the second dose varies considerably across countries, ranging from early in the second 
615: year of life in Austria and Germany to preschool or primary school ages elsewhere. Additionally, catch-up 
616: recommendations vary widely, with Spain, for example, extending vaccination opportunities up to 64 years of age [15].
617: 
618: ---
619: 
620: Modelling studies suggest that in countries with substantial immunity gaps, supplementary immunisation strategies 
621: targeting individuals not covered by existing programmes may be required to achieve interruption of measles 
622: transmission [16].
623: 
624: The latest WHO estimates on national immunisation coverage for 2023 show a slight overall decrease in 
625: vaccination coverage within the EU/EEA compared to previous years; however, the estimates remained relatively 
626: consistent over the last five years. In 2023, the overall weighted vaccination coverage in the EU/EEA was 93.9% 
627: for the first dose (MCV1) and 88.8% for the second dose (MCV2). Six countries reported decreased coverage for 
628: the first measles vaccine dose, with Romania experiencing the most significant reduction (from 83% in 2022 to 
629: 78% in 2023). Similarly, nine countries reported decreased coverage for the second dose. While fifteen EU/EEA 
630: countries (50%) reached the ≥95% threshold for the first vaccine dose, only four countries (14%)—Hungary, 
631: Malta, Portugal, and Slovakia—achieved this threshold for the second dose. This represents a decline compared to 
632: the seven countries (Bulgaria, Hungary, Latvia, Malta, Norway, Portugal, and Slovakia) meeting the ≥95% 
633: benchmark for MCV2 in 2019, highlighting persistent challenges in attaining optimal vaccination coverage required 
634: for measles elimination. It is also to be noted that in two countries there was a positive upward trend of 3% or 
635: above (range up to 7%) when comparing the estimates from 2020 to 2023 for the first dose, and an upward trend 
636: in four countries for the second dose. A downward trend of 3% or more was observed in eight countries, both for 
637: the first and the second dose.
638: 
639: The European Regional Verification Commission for Measles and Rubella Elimination (RVC), which was established 
640: in 2011 [13] monitors the progress of the countries of the WHO European Region in relation to measles and rubella 
641: elimination. During the 12th RCV meeting, held in 2023, with reference to the data of 2022, it was concluded that 
642: 20 EU/EEA Member States provided evidence to demonstrate the elimination of endemic measles, whereas five 
643: countries were considered endemic, three countries were considered to have re-established measles transmission 
644: and for one country, the status is still pending [16].
645: 
646: ### Public health implications
647: 
648: ECDC continues to closely monitor measles activity in the EU/EEA, providing monthly epidemiological updates and 
649: assessments to support Member States' public health actions. ECDC continues to recommend the following actions 
650: for a public health response: closing immunity gaps through achieving and maintaining ≥95% vaccination coverage 
651: with two doses of measles-containing vaccine, enhancing surveillance quality, ensuring rapid detection, diagnosis, 
652: and outbreak control, and raising clinical awareness among healthcare providers. The deployment of upgraded 
653: digitalised immunisation information systems to identify and reach the unvaccinated is also critical and should form
654: an integral part of national efforts to improve the performance and management.
655: 
656: ### Conclusion
657: 
658: In 2024, the EU/EEA region recorded the highest number of measles cases observed in the past two decades, 
659: significantly exceeding pre-pandemic levels. This sharp increase underscores persistent immunity gaps and 
660: vulnerabilities within the population, exacerbated by suboptimal measles vaccination coverage. Although the 
661: impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on immunisation programmes varied by country — with some experiencing 
662: declines and others maintaining or slightly improving coverage — most EU/EEA countries have yet to achieve or 
663: sustain the ≥95% vaccination coverage target with two doses of measles-containing vaccine. Enhanced 
664: epidemiological surveillance, prompt outbreak investigation, and control measures remain critical for interrupting 
665: transmission and achieving regional elimination targets. Urgent action to address existing immunity gaps through 
666: targeted catch-up vaccination campaigns, particularly among populations disproportionately impacted by pandemic 
667: disruptions are essential. Strengthened public health communication and accelerated efforts to enhance vaccine 
668: acceptance remain crucial for restoring high immunisation coverage and preventing future measles outbreaks in 
669: the EU/EEA.

52: ### Introduction
53: 
54: Measles is an acute, highly contagious viral disease capable of causing epidemics. It is caused by a single-stranded 
55: ribonucleic acid (RNA) virus of the genus Morbillivirus and the family Paramyxoviridae. The virus is transmitted 
56: from person-to-person via respiratory droplets produced when infected people cough and sneeze. Virus-containing 
57: droplets can remain in the air for several hours, and the virus remains infectious on contaminated surfaces for up 
58: to two hours [1]. It is characterised by symptoms such as high fever, cough, runny nose, inflamed eyes, and a 
59: distinctive red rash that spreads across the body. Complications can be severe and include pneumonia, hearing 
60: loss, encephalitis, and death [1].
61: 
62: Measles is extremely infectious and it is estimated that 90% of non-immune people exposed to an individual with 
63: the infection will contract the disease. Mathematical models estimate the basic reproductive number at 12–18, i.e. 
64: the average number of secondary infections that follow a single introduction into a susceptible population.
65: Immunisation against measles started in the 1960s and has dramatically reduced the incidence of measles in 
66: Europe. But despite overall high immunisation coverage, measles continues to circulate. Globally, measles remains 
67: a leading cause of childhood death, and an estimated 140 000 children die each year from complications caused by 
68: the disease.
69: 
70: Measles prevention at the individual level requires two doses of a measles-containing vaccine (MCV). At population 
71: level, achieving and sustaining a vaccination coverage of at least 95% with two doses is essential to control the 
72: spread of the disease and prevent outbreaks. Immunisation remains the cornerstone of measles control and 
73: outbreak prevention [1, 2].
74: 
75: ### Methods
76: 
77: This report is based on data for 2024 retrieved from EpiPulse Cases on 20 March 2025. EpiPulse Cases is a newly 
78: introduced system for the collection, analysis and dissemination of data on communicable diseases that replaced 
79: The European Surveillance System (TESSy) in October 2024.
80: 
81: For a detailed description of methods used to produce this report, please refer to the ‘Methods’ chapter [3]. An 
82: overview of the national surveillance systems is available online [4].
83: 
84: A subset of the data used for this report is available through ECDC’s online ‘Surveillance atlas of infectious 
85: diseases’[5] and the Monthly Measles and Rubella Reports [6] where additional information may also be found in 
86: relation to surveillance systems and historical changes to surveillance, as well as possibility to download datasets
87: and additional visualisations.
88: 
89: ECDC has coordinated the surveillance of measles at the European level since the transfer of EUVAC.NET 
90: (European surveillance network for selected vaccine-preventable diseases, hosted by Statens Serum Institute, 
91: Denmark) to ECDC in 2011. Thirty European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA) Member States report 
92: measles data to ECDC. The 2008, 2012, or 2018 EU case definition [4, 7] are used by 27 countries and the 
93: majority report data from comprehensive, passive surveillance systems with national coverage. Belgium has
94: reported aggregated data since 2017, and Poland from (and including) April 2019. Up to December 2020, thirty 
95: countries (29 EU countries plus the UK) reported measles data on a routine basis. The United Kingdom (UK) 
96: stopped reporting measles cases to TESSy in December 2020<sup>1</sup>.
97: 
98: Data submitted by EU/EEA Member States are shared with the WHO Regional Office for Europe monthly as part of 
99: the measles surveillance of the WHO European Region. Vaccination coverage estimates presented in this report 
100: were obtained from the WHO Global Health Observatory website, WUENIC estimates [8]. The method of 
101: calculating MCV1 and MCV2 coverage are outlined in the metadata available for each indicator online [9].
102: 
103: ### Epidemiology
104: 
105: In the EU/EEA, measles activity began to increase in 2023 after a period of unusually low activity during 2020–
106: 2022, coinciding with the COVID-19 pandemic [2]. In 2024, a total of 35 212 cases of measles were reported 
107: across the EU/EEA, marking a notable increase from the 3 973 cases reported in 2023. All 28 EU/EEA countries 
108: reported measles activity in 2024, and two countries (Latvia and Liechtenstein) reported zero cases (Table 1, 
109: Figure 1). Romania accounted for the vast majority of reported cases (87%), with a total of 30 692 cases. The 
110: overall notification rate increased significantly in 2024 to 77.4 cases per 1 000 000 population, compared to 9.1 in 
111: 2023, 0.3 in 2022, 0.2 in 2021, and 4.6 in 2020, and it was also higher than the pre-pandemic rate in 2019 (27.2)
112: [10] (Table 1, Figure 1).
113: 
114: <sup>1</sup>The United Kingdom (UK) was a former Member State of the European Union (EU). The UK withdrew from the EU on 31 
115: January 2020, but continued reporting measles cases to TESSy till December 2020.

120: 1 610.7 cases per 1 000 000 population in Romania. Other countries reporting high notification rates included

122:

124: exceeded the total number of cases reported in 2019 (pre COVID-19), which was 12 320 cases [10].

234: #### Seasonality and trend
235: 
236: In 2024, measles epidemiology returned to its typical seasonal pattern within the EU/EEA, with the highest number 
237: of cases reported from February to July, followed by a gradual decline during the second half of the year (Figure 
238: 3). This contrasts with 2023, when measles activity did not follow the usual seasonality pattern and instead 
239: increased predominantly in the latter half of the year, diverging from the expected epidemiological trend. The 
240: marked resurgence in 2024 emphasises a return to more typical measles seasonal patterns, but at significantly 
241: elevated levels compared to the pandemic and pre-pandemic years (Figure 4).

286: #### Age distribution:
287: 
288: In 2024, of the 35 212 measles cases reported, infants under one year of age remained the most affected group, 
289: with a notably high notification rate of 1 175.4 cases per 1 000 000 population (13%). The next most affected 
290: groups were children aged 1–4 years with a notification rate of 688.7 cases per 1 000 000 (33.1%), followed by 
291: children aged 5–9 years with a rate of 247.1 cases per 1 000 000 (16%). The rates progressively decreased with 
292: age, recording 169.9 per 1 000 000 among 10–14-year-olds (11.6%), 129.4 per 1 000 000 in the 15–19 age group
293: (8.8%), 45.8 per 1 000 000 among young adults aged 20–29 years (6.5%), and 12.2 per 1 000 000 in individuals 
294: aged 30 years and older (10.9%) (Figure 5). Overall, 26.3% of cases were above 14 years of age and 46.1% were 
295: below the age of five years which highlights the fact that measles affects all age groups.
296: 
297: The median age of cases across all EU/EEA countries that submitted age-based data in 2024 was five years of age 
298: (interquartile range, IQR:2-15), corresponding to 2023, where the median age was 5 as well, while the IQR was 2-
299: 12. In 2024, as was the case in 2023, the overall age distribution of cases was heavily influenced by the high 
300: number of cases in Romania. In Romania the majority of cases were reported among the 1-4 years old age group
301: accounting for 35.5% of the total cases. In contrast, in several EU/EEA countries the majority of cases reported
302: were among the +30-age group (France: 28.4%, Poland: 34.4%, Spain: 38.5%, Italy: 52.4%).

320: ### Vaccination status
321: 
322: Data on vaccination status were available for 31 804 cases (90%) reported in 2024. Of these cases, 27 692 (87%) 
323: were unvaccinated, 2 692 (8%) were vaccinated with one dose of measles-containing vaccine, 1 374 (4%) were 
324: vaccinated with two or more doses, and 46 cases (0.1%) were vaccinated with an unknown number of doses 
325: (Figure 6). The proportion of reported unvaccinated cases for 2024 was the highest observed in the last five years.
326: 
327: Among cases with known vaccination status, the highest proportion of unvaccinated cases by age group was those 
328: aged <1 year (98%), a group not routinely targeted with measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccination in most 
329: countries, followed by those aged 1–4 years (90%), 5–9 years (84%), and 10-14 years (80%), 15-19 years (78%), 
330: 20-29 years (83%), and for +30 years (87%). Vaccination status was more likely to be unknown with increasing 
331: age, accounting for 28% and 24% of cases aged 30+ years and 20–29 years, respectively.
332: 
333: ---
334: 
335: For the years 2019–2023, the overall distribution of cases by age group and vaccination status followed the same 
336: pattern, with the unvaccinated population of 0–9 years and >20 years of age counting for approximately 80% of 
337: the total number of cases (Figure 7).
338: 
339: The proportion of children aged 1–4 years who were unvaccinated in 2024 (90%) remained equally high compared 
340: to 2023 (88%) and to what was observed in the period 2019–2022, when 80% of children of this age group were 
341: unvaccinated and 98% of children aged <1 year were unvaccinated.
342: 
343: When vaccination status was known and in relation to younger adults (>14 years) and adults >20 years, the 
344: majority were not vaccinated or not fully vaccinated (82% and 85% respectively unvaccinated, and 9% and 7%
345: respectively vaccinated only with one dose).

379: #### Vaccination coverage
380: 
381: Data on vaccination coverage for the first and second dose of measles-containing vaccine were available up to 
382: 2023. In 2023, the overall population weighted vaccination coverage for the EU/EEA countries was 93.9% for the 
383: first dose and 88.8% for the second dose, which represents a slight decrease compared to previous years (Table 
384: 2). Six countries reported a decrease in the vaccination coverage for the first dose of measles in 2023 compared to 
385: the coverage reported in 2022, (the highest decrease was reported in Romania (83% in 2022, and 78 in 2023))
386: and an additional nine countries reported a decrease in coverage for the second dose. Moreover, three countries 
387: reported an increase in vaccination coverage for dose one (range 1-2%) and four countries for dose two (1-3%). 
388: Fifteen countries (50%) reported a coverage of ≥95% for dose one and only four countries (14%) (Hungary, 
389: Malta, Portugal, and Slovakia) had a coverage of ≥95% for the second dose (Figure 8, Figure 9). Only three
390: countries had an estimated coverage of ≥95% for both MCV1 and MCV2 in 2023 (Hungary, Malta, and Portugal).
391: 
392: The percent of change in vaccination coverage between 2020 and 2023 showed some variation. While Austria 
393: demonstrated the largest percentage of improvement for the second dose (+6%), Romania experienced the 
394: sharpest decline in both doses (–9% for dose one, –13% for dose two). A total of 16 countries showed a decrease 
395: in coverage for at least one dose, with declines more pronounced for dose two. The overall EU/EEA vaccination 
396: coverage average dropped slightly by 0.5% for MCV1 and 0.8% for MCV2 in 2023 compared to 2020. (Table 2)
397: 
398: #### Outcome
399: 
400: In 2024, the disease outcome was reported for 31 430 cases (89% of total cases). There were 23 deaths 
401: attributable to measles, which was a significant increase compared to previous years. Romania reported the 
402: majority of these deaths (22 deaths), with one additional death reported from Ireland. In comparison, three deaths 
403: were reported in 2023 retrospectively, and no deaths were reported in the preceding two years (2021–2022), while 
404: two deaths occurred in 2020 and ten deaths were recorded in 2019 in EU/EEA countries. This highlights a 
405: resurgence in severe measles outcomes in 2024.
406: 
407: When considering the age of the deaths, five cases were in children <1 year old, nine deaths in children between 
408: 1-4 years, two deaths in adults between 20-29 years, and seven deaths in the age group over 30 years of age. 
409: Sixteen of those who died where unvaccinated, five had only one dose, and two people had unknown vaccination status.
410: 
411: #### Hospitalisation and complications
412: 
413: Hospitalisation status was available for 31 035 (88%) cases, of which 24 529 (79%) were hospitalised in 2024. 
414: Among the hospitalised cases, 20 095 (82%) were unvaccinated. 1 809 (7%) individuals had received one dose of 
415: measles-containing vaccine, 739 (3%) individuals had received two or more doses, and 1 886 (8%) individuals had 
416: unknown vaccination status. The most hospitalised cases (96%) were reported by Romania. The median age of 
417: hospitalised cases reported in the EU/EEA was five years (IQR: 2-15 years).
418: 
419: Among all reported cases in 2024, data on complications were reported for 24 239 (68%) cases, 1 483 of which 
420: (6%) had no complications. Reported complications included 6 769 (28%) cases of pneumonia, 187 cases of 
421: diarrhoea, 19 cases of otitis media and 10 cases of acute encephalitis. Unspecified complications (‘other’) were 
422: reported for 15 744 (64.9%) cases. Of these 24 239 cases reported with complications, 19 420 (80%) cases were 
423: unvaccinated. The median age of the cases presented with complications was five years (IQR: 2–15 years).
424: 
425: #### Importations
426: 
427: In 2024, importation status was available for 2 866 (8%) cases. Of these cases, 542 (18%) were classified as 
428: imported in 2024 and 222 as import-related (7%) meaning the source of infection (exposure) was outside the 
429: reporting country. Twenty-six countries reported imported measles cases for 2024, the majority of which were 
430: reported by Austria (44), Germany (81), Spain (54), France (86), Italy (52), and Romania (39), accounting for 65% 
431: of all imported cases. The median age of these cases was five years (range 0–91 years).
432: 
433: Among the 542 imported cases for which a single probable country of infection was available, most individuals
434: were thought to have acquired their infection in Europe (EU/EEA: 26%, non-EU/EEA: 39%), followed by Asia 
435: (22%), and Africa (4%). An unknown origin of infection was reported for 8% of the cases. Of the 68 different 
436: countries listed as the likely origin of infection of imported cases, five countries accounted for 50% of these 
437: infections: Romania (122), Morocco (53), UK (36), Bosnia and Herzegovina (35), and Italy (25).
438: 
439: The proportion of imported measles cases for 2024 appeared to be higher than 2023 and 2022; 128 (5%) cases 
440: and 22 (18%) cases respectively, and higher than the pre-pandemic period as well, which was 62 (3%) cases in 
441: 2020, 644 (5%) cases in 2019.
